subtopic: Factuality, citation and source attribution evaluation
title: Long-form factuality in large language models
publisher: NeurIPS 2024 (poster); Wei, Yang, Song, Lu, Hu, Huang, Tran, Peng, Liu, Huang, Du, Le (Google DeepMind)

key_points.claim: LongFact is a benchmark prompt set, generated with GPT-4, for testing long-form factuality in open domains: thousands of questions across 38 topics.
key_points.evidence_quote: we first use GPT-4 to generate LongFact, a prompt set comprising thousands of questions spanning 38 topics

key_points.claim: The paper proposes SAFE, which uses LLM agents as automated evaluators of long-form factuality.
key_points.evidence_quote: we propose that LLM agents can be used as automated evaluators for long-form factuality through a method which we call Search-Augmented Factuality Evaluator (SAFE)

key_points.claim: SAFE's method: split a response into individual facts, then check each one through multi-step reasoning using Google Search queries.
key_points.evidence_quote: SAFE utilizes an LLM to break down a long-form response into a set of individual facts and to evaluate the accuracy of each fact using a multi-step reasoning process comprising sending search queries to Google Search and determining whether a fact is supported by the search results

key_points.claim: The paper proposes an extended F1 metric (F1@K). Precision is the share of supported facts. Recall is measured against a hyperparameter for the user's preferred response length, so both accuracy and coverage count.
key_points.evidence_quote: we balance the percentage of supported facts in a response (precision) with the percentage of provided facts relative to a hyperparameter representing a user’s preferred response length (recall)

key_points.claim: SAFE agreed with crowdsourced human annotators 72% of the time on about 16k facts. On 100 randomly sampled disagreement cases, SAFE was judged correct 76% of the time.
key_points.evidence_quote: on a set of∼16k individual facts, SAFE agrees with crowdsourced human annotators 72% of the time, and on a random subset of 100 disagreement cases, SAFE wins 76% of the time

key_points.claim: SAFE costs more than 20 times less than human annotation.
key_points.evidence_quote: SAFE is more than 20 times cheaper than human annotators

key_points.claim: Across 13 models from four families, larger models generally scored better on long-form factuality.
key_points.evidence_quote: We also benchmark thirteen language models on LongFact across four model families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, and PaLM-2), finding that larger language models generally achieve better long-form factuality

key_points.claim: The benchmark, evaluator and code are released openly, so results can be reproduced.
key_points.evidence_quote: LongFact, SAFE, and all experimental code are available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/long-form-factuality

reliability_notes: This is a peer-reviewed NeurIPS 2024 paper from Google DeepMind; only the abstract page was fetched. It is about evaluating the factuality of long-form LLM output, not research agents directly. Still, the method (breaking output into atomic facts, checking them with search-augmented LLM agents, and scoring precision/recall with F1@K) applies to judging research-agent reports. The claim that SAFE beats humans is based on only 100 disagreement cases, and the 72% agreement figure comes from crowdsourced annotators, not experts. The 2024 results may be dated.
